newsitem.title: USA: Takeout dining replacing meals from scratch in US.
newsitem.headline: Takeout dining replacing meals from scratch in US.

text.p: Americans are depending more and more on professional chefs to aid them at meal times, but are not eating more meals in restaurants, a market research group says.
Restaurant chefs have become many families' private cooks -- thanks to the takeout container, says The NPD Group in its 11th annual Report on Eating Patterns in America.
"The way we eat is changing, and many of those changes centre around the continual desire for convenience," said NPD Vice President Harry Balzer.
However, the report implys that Americans are spending increasing amounts per meal because takeout foods cost much more than the raw ingredients, if the same meal were prepared at home.

According to the NPD report, only 55 percent of American dinners last year contained at least one item made from scratch, down from 64 percent 10 years ago. Last year, only 11.3 percent of breakfasts contained at least one completely homemade dish, down from 16 percent in 1985.

The number of additives, ingredients and cooking aids used per main meal is also at an all-time low, NPD reported. Homemade items are down at breakfast and lunch, resulting, in general, in a decline in the number of items used to prepare meals, it said.
Dinner eaters are less likely than ever before to eat side dishes, desserts or beverages with their meal. An entree is now the "only stable part of a meal," Balzer said.

Vegetables, part of more than half of all dinners in 1987, now are served at only 43 percent. Potatoes, served last year at 23 percent of dinners, were served at 28 percent of dinners in 1987. Salads were served at 16 percent of dinners, down from 19 percent of meals in 1987 and breads, served at 10 percent of meals in 1996, were served at 13 percent of meals in 1987.

According to the report on eating patterns, leftovers have become an American way of life. More and more cooks feel that if they're going to prepare a meal, they might as well get more than one meal out of the effort. Today, more than one in 10 main meals consist of leftovers. This is up nearly 30 percent over the past 10 years.
Relying on a professional chef at meal time has increased dramatically, but in-restaurant dining has not, the report states.

"Restaurants are becoming prepared food supermarkets," Balzer said, and takeout is a booming business. During the past 10 years, the number of takeout meals per capita has jumped to 65 in 1996 from 48 in 1986. The total number of takeout suppers prepared by restaurants has doubled during the period.
On-premise dining has fallen only slightly to 63 per capita last year from 68 in 1986.
